title: Best Antacid After Drinking: Tums vs Pepcid vs Gaviscon vs Prilosec
excerpt: Which antacid works best after drinking? An honest comparison of Tums, Mylanta, Gaviscon, Pepcid, and Prilosec, what to avoid, and the red flags that need a doctor.
metaDescription: Best antacid after drinking: Tums vs Mylanta vs Gaviscon vs Pepcid vs Prilosec, which to avoid (Alka-Seltzer), and red flags like vomiting blood.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** for occasional heartburn or a sour, burning stomach after a night of drinking, a plain chewable antacid like Tums (calcium carbonate) or a liquid like Mylanta is usually the fastest, simplest choice. If acid keeps creeping up your throat when you lie down, an alginate product like Gaviscon tends to work better because it forms a barrier on top of your stomach contents. If you know a big night tends to give you heartburn, famotidine (Pepcid AC) taken *before* you start drinking is the better tool, because it lowers acid production for hours. Omeprazole (Prilosec OTC) is the strongest of the group, but it is not a quick fix and is designed for a 14-day course, not a single rough morning.

**The one to avoid:** Original Alka-Seltzer and similar fizzy "upset stomach plus headache" tablets contain **aspirin**. Aspirin and alcohol together raise the risk of stomach irritation and bleeding, which is the opposite of what an irritated stomach needs. Pepto-Bismol contains a related salicylate, so it isn't a clean swap either.

> **This is not medical advice.** This guide explains how common over-the-counter stomach medicines work and what their labels say. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history and the other medicines you take. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before using these products if** you have kidney disease, heart failure, high blood pressure on a low-sodium diet, a history of ulcers or stomach bleeding, or you take prescription medicines (many drugs are absorbed differently when taken with antacids). **Get emergency care right away** if you vomit blood or material that looks like coffee grounds, pass black or tarry stools, have severe or worsening belly pain, or have chest pain, especially pain that spreads to the arm, jaw, or back, or comes with shortness of breath or sweating. Heartburn and a heart attack can feel alike. In the US, call 911.

## Why Your Stomach Burns After Drinking

It helps to know what you're treating, because the different medicines target different parts of the problem. Alcohol upsets your upper digestive tract in three main ways.

**1. It relaxes the valve at the top of your stomach.** A ring of muscle called the lower esophageal sphincter normally keeps stomach contents where they belong. Alcohol loosens it. When that valve relaxes, acid can wash back up into your esophagus, which is what you feel as heartburn or acid reflux. This is why the burning is often worst after you lie down in bed.

**2. Some drinks push your stomach to make more acid.** Beer and wine, in particular, have been shown in older physiology studies to stimulate stomach acid more strongly than distilled spirits. Carbonated mixers can add pressure that encourages reflux. Late-night greasy food adds to it, because fatty meals sit in the stomach longer and also relax that valve.

**3. Alcohol irritates the stomach lining directly.** A heavy session can inflame the lining of the stomach, a condition called acute gastritis. This produces a gnawing, burning, or sore feeling in the upper middle of your belly, often with nausea. It isn't only about acid splashing upward. The lining itself is sore, and acid touching an irritated surface hurts more.

So the right product depends on which of these is bothering you most. Neutralizing acid helps all three a little. Blocking acid helps most if you plan ahead. A physical barrier helps most when reflux into the throat is the main issue. Our [heartburn after drinking guide](/never-hungover/heartburn-after-drinking) goes deeper on the worst drinks and habits that trigger it.

## The Main Types of Antacid and Acid Reducer, Compared

People say "antacid" for anything that calms a burning stomach, but there are really four different kinds of product on the shelf. They work in different ways and on different timelines.

| Type | Common brands | How it works | How fast | How long it lasts | Best use after drinking |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Calcium carbonate antacid | Tums, Rolaids (some versions), store brands | Neutralizes acid already in the stomach | Within minutes | Short, often an hour or two | Quick relief for occasional heartburn or sour stomach |
| Aluminum/magnesium antacid | Mylanta, Maalox (some versions), store-brand liquids | Neutralizes acid; liquids coat quickly | Within minutes | Short | Fast relief, especially if you prefer a liquid |
| Alginate plus antacid | Gaviscon | Forms a foam "raft" on top of stomach contents that helps block reflux, plus neutralizes acid | Within minutes | Somewhat longer than plain antacids for reflux | Acid coming up your throat, especially at bedtime |
| H2 blocker | Famotidine (Pepcid AC), store brands | Lowers how much acid your stomach produces | Usually within an hour | Several hours | Taken *before* drinking if you know you'll get heartburn |
| Proton pump inhibitor (PPI) | Omeprazole (Prilosec OTC), esomeprazole (Nexium 24HR), lansoprazole (Prevacid 24HR) | Shuts down the stomach's acid pumps | Slow; full effect can take a few days | About a day per dose | Frequent heartburn on a doctor's or label's 14-day plan, not a one-off night |

There are also **combination products**. Pepcid Complete, for example, pairs famotidine with calcium carbonate and magnesium hydroxide, so you get fast neutralizing plus longer acid reduction in one chew.

Now let's go through each one in plain terms.

## Tums After Drinking: Fast, Cheap, and Usually Fine

Tums is calcium carbonate, a simple base that reacts with stomach acid and neutralizes it. There's no known dangerous interaction between calcium carbonate and alcohol, which is why it's a sensible first reach for occasional heartburn after a few drinks.

**Pros**

- Works within minutes.
- Inexpensive and easy to find.
- No meaningful interaction with alcohol itself.

**Cons**

- Relief is short. If you have a long night of reflux ahead, you may need more than one dose, and it's easy to lose count.
- It's easy to take too many. Each Tums label sets a daily maximum that depends on the strength, and you should not exceed it. Very large amounts of calcium over time can raise blood calcium, and in rare cases cause a condition called milk-alkali syndrome, which can affect the kidneys.
- Some people notice their acid "bounces back" after the effect wears off.
- Calcium can constipate.

**Best for:** a social drinker who gets a bit of heartburn now and then and wants something quick. If you want the full detail on dosing and timing, see our [Tums and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tums-and-alcohol).

## Mylanta and Maalox-Style Liquids: Fast Relief, Watch the Side Effects

Classic liquid antacids like Mylanta combine **aluminum hydroxide** and **magnesium hydroxide**, often with simethicone for gas. Formulas change between brands and over time, so always read the Drug Facts box on the bottle you actually own.

The pairing is deliberate. Magnesium tends to loosen stools and aluminum tends to firm them, so together they roughly balance out. In practice, some people still get diarrhea from the magnesium, which is worth knowing if alcohol already sends you running to the bathroom.

**Pros**

- Liquids coat and neutralize quickly, which many people find soothing for a raw, burning stomach.
- Some versions include simethicone, which may help if you feel bloated from beer or fizzy mixers.

**Cons**

- Magnesium can cause diarrhea.
- People with **kidney disease** should ask a doctor before using aluminum or magnesium antacids, because the kidneys have to clear these minerals.
- Like all antacids, the relief is short.

**Best for:** people who prefer a liquid and want fast relief for a sour, burning stomach. If drinking already gives you loose stools, a calcium-based chew may suit you better.

## Gaviscon: The Pick When Acid Keeps Coming Up Your Throat

Gaviscon is different from a plain antacid because many of its formulas contain an **alginate**, a substance that comes from seaweed. When it meets stomach acid, it forms a thick foam that floats on top of your stomach contents like a raft. That raft physically helps keep acid from washing back up into your esophagus. Gaviscon also contains antacid ingredients that neutralize acid.

The exact ingredients differ between the US and UK versions and between the liquid and tablet forms, so check the box. The alginate is the part that makes Gaviscon stand out.

**Pros**

- Especially useful for reflux symptoms: burning in the chest or throat, a sour taste in your mouth, or acid coming up when you lie down. That's a classic after-drinking pattern.
- Starts working quickly.

**Cons**

- Some versions are high in sodium, which matters if you're on a low-sodium diet for blood pressure or heart failure.
- Contains aluminum and magnesium ingredients in some formulas, with the same kidney caution as Mylanta.
- Less helpful if your main problem is a sore, gnawing stomach rather than reflux.

**Best for:** the "I lay down and now my throat is on fire" situation. Take it after your last drink and before bed, following the label. Propping your head up on an extra pillow helps too.

## Pepcid (Famotidine): Best When You Plan Ahead

Famotidine is an **H2 blocker**. Instead of neutralizing acid that's already there, it tells the stomach to make less acid in the first place. It takes longer to kick in than Tums, usually within an hour, but it lasts several hours.

That makes it a good fit for a specific situation: you know beer, wine, or a big dinner out reliably gives you heartburn, so you take it beforehand. The Pepcid AC label includes directions for preventing heartburn by taking it before eating food or drinking beverages that cause heartburn, and it sets a daily maximum. Follow those directions rather than guessing.

### Does Pepcid raise your blood alcohol?

This is a fair question, because some older acid reducers in the same family (cimetidine and ranitidine) were shown in some studies to slightly raise blood alcohol levels by reducing how much alcohol the stomach breaks down before it reaches the bloodstream. Studies on famotidine have generally not found a meaningful effect of this kind. Either way, no acid reducer should change how much you drink. Our [Pepcid and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/pepcid-and-alcohol) covers this in detail.

**Pros**

- Longer-lasting than antacids.
- Works well when taken ahead of time.
- Not a dangerous combination with moderate drinking for most healthy adults.

**Cons**

- Slower to start, so it's not the best rescue for heartburn that's already blazing (a combination product like Pepcid Complete, or a Tums alongside it, covers the gap).
- Lowering acid does nothing for the direct irritation alcohol causes. It can make you feel fine while you keep drinking.
- If you need it most weeks, that's a sign to talk to a doctor.

**Best for:** people who get predictable heartburn from drinking and want to head it off.

Some people also use famotidine, often with an antihistamine, to reduce facial flushing from alcohol. That is a different use with a different set of concerns. We explain it in a separate guide on [Pepcid for Asian flush](/never-hungover/pepcid-for-asian-flush).

## Prilosec and Nexium (PPIs): Powerful, but Not a Hangover Fix

Omeprazole (Prilosec OTC), esomeprazole (Nexium 24HR), and lansoprazole (Prevacid 24HR) are **proton pump inhibitors**. They shut down the tiny pumps in your stomach lining that release acid. They're the strongest acid reducers you can buy without a prescription.

The catch is timing. The over-the-counter labels describe these as a **14-day course for frequent heartburn** (heartburn on two or more days a week), and they say they're not meant for immediate relief. A PPI you take the morning after drinking won't do much for the burn you feel right now. It can take a few days to reach its full effect.

**Pros**

- Very effective for frequent heartburn when used as directed.
- Once-a-day dosing.

**Cons**

- Not for fast relief.
- Not designed for a one-off night out.
- Longer-term use should be supervised by a doctor, who can weigh benefits against possible downsides.

**Best for:** people who have heartburn often, whether or not they've been drinking, and are following the label's 14-day plan or a doctor's advice. If you need a PPI to tolerate your usual drinking, that's worth a conversation with your doctor. See our [omeprazole and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/omeprazole-and-alcohol) for more.

## What About Alka-Seltzer, Pepto-Bismol, and Baking Soda?

These three often end up in the same cabinet, so they're worth sorting out.

### Original Alka-Seltzer: skip it after drinking

Original Alka-Seltzer is a fizzing tablet that contains **aspirin**, sodium bicarbonate, and citric acid. It's marketed for heartburn and acid indigestion *with* headache or body aches, which sounds tailor-made for a hangover. The problem is the aspirin. Aspirin and other NSAID painkillers carry a label warning about stomach bleeding for people who have three or more drinks a day, and alcohol already irritates the stomach lining. Adding aspirin to an inflamed stomach is not a good trade.

Alka-Seltzer also makes products that don't contain aspirin, such as its heartburn-relief versions, and some cold-and-flu versions contain other drugs entirely. Read the Drug Facts box carefully. Our [aspirin and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/aspirin-and-alcohol) explains the bleeding risk.

### Pepto-Bismol: not really an antacid

Pepto-Bismol is bismuth subsalicylate. It's mainly used for nausea, upset stomach, and diarrhea. The "salicylate" part is a chemical cousin of aspirin, so the same general caution about stomach irritation and bleeding applies, and people who are allergic to aspirin or take blood thinners should avoid it unless a doctor says otherwise. It can also turn your tongue or stool black, which is harmless but can be confused with bleeding. More in our [Pepto-Bismol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/pepto-bismol-and-alcohol).

### Baking soda: an old trick with real downsides

A half-teaspoon of baking soda (sodium bicarbonate) in water does neutralize acid. But it's very high in sodium, it releases gas as it reacts, and there are rare case reports of the stomach rupturing when people took baking soda on a very full stomach, such as after a big meal and a lot of drinks. A labeled antacid is a better choice.

## The Best Antacid for a Hangover

If you wake up with a sour stomach, nausea, and a headache, it's tempting to look for one product that handles all of it. There isn't one, and the products that promise to do it often contain aspirin.

A more sensible approach:

1. **For the stomach:** a calcium carbonate chew (Tums) or a liquid antacid (Mylanta) for fast relief, or Gaviscon if the main issue is acid in your throat.
2. **For the headache:** be careful. Aspirin and ibuprofen are harder on an irritated stomach. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) is gentler on the stomach but has its own liver concerns with alcohol, which we explain in our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol). Eat something first, and use a single standard dose of whatever you choose.
3. **For the nausea and dehydration:** sip water or an electrolyte drink slowly, and try bland food like toast, crackers, or rice once you can keep it down. Our [hangover nausea guide](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) covers this step by step.

Antacids treat the burning. They don't speed up how fast your body clears alcohol, and they don't fix the other parts of a hangover.

## The Best Antacid for Alcohol Gastritis

If your main symptom is a gnawing, aching, or burning pain in the upper middle of your belly, sometimes with nausea or a feeling of being full quickly, the lining of your stomach may be inflamed. This is often called alcohol gastritis.

For a mild, short-lived episode after one heavy night:

- **An antacid** (Tums or a liquid like Mylanta) can ease the burn quickly.
- **An H2 blocker** like famotidine can reduce acid for longer, which gives the lining a gentler environment while it settles.
- **Stopping alcohol** for a few days matters more than any pill. Antacids don't heal the irritation. Time without alcohol does.
- **Avoid aspirin and ibuprofen-type painkillers**, which can irritate the lining further.

If the pain lasts more than a few days, keeps coming back every time you drink, or comes with any of the red flags below, see a doctor. Ongoing gastritis can lead to ulcers, and a doctor may test for a common stomach bacteria (*H. pylori*) that causes similar symptoms. Our [stomach pain after drinking guide](/never-hungover/stomach-pain-after-drinking) explains the different causes of upper-belly pain.

## Can You Take an Antacid While You're Still Drinking?

You can take a calcium carbonate antacid like Tums during a night out without a known dangerous interaction. But there are a few things to keep in mind:

- **It can hide a warning sign.** Heartburn is partly your body's way of telling you the stomach is unhappy. Masking it so you can keep drinking just moves the problem to the morning.
- **Count your doses.** It's easy to chew a few Tums every hour and blow past the label's daily limit without noticing, especially after a few drinks.
- **If you know you'll need it, plan ahead instead.** Taking famotidine before you go out, following the label, usually works better than chewing antacids all night.

## Interactions to Know About

Antacids are simple, but they can still get in the way of other medicines.

- **They can block absorption of some drugs.** Antacids can reduce how well your body absorbs certain antibiotics (such as tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones like ciprofloxacin), thyroid medicine (levothyroxine), and iron supplements, among others. Pharmacists commonly advise spacing doses a few hours apart. If you take any regular prescription, ask your pharmacist how to time an antacid around it.
- **Kidney disease:** aluminum- and magnesium-containing antacids, and large amounts of calcium, should be used only with a doctor's okay.
- **Low-sodium diets:** some antacids, Alka-Seltzer, and baking soda are high in sodium.
- **Stacking products:** combination products like Pepcid Complete already contain antacid ingredients. Don't add Tums on top without checking the totals.

## Red Flags: When Stomach Pain After Drinking Needs a Doctor

Most heartburn after a night of drinking is uncomfortable but harmless and settles within a day. Some symptoms are not something to treat with an antacid. These can point to bleeding, a tear, an ulcer, or inflammation of the pancreas.

**Go to the emergency room or call 911 if you have:**

- **Vomiting blood**, whether bright red or dark material that looks like coffee grounds. Forceful vomiting after drinking can tear the lining where the esophagus meets the stomach (a Mallory-Weiss tear), and ulcers can bleed. Our guide on [vomiting blood after drinking](/never-hungover/vomiting-blood-after-drinking) explains what to do.
- **Black, tarry, or bloody stools.** This can be a sign of bleeding higher up in the gut. (Pepto-Bismol can also turn stool black, but if you aren't sure, get checked.)
- **Severe belly pain, especially pain that bores through to your back,** often with vomiting. This can be a sign of pancreatitis, which heavy drinking can trigger.
- **Chest pain or pressure,** particularly with shortness of breath, sweating, or pain in the arm, jaw, or back. Don't assume it's heartburn.
- **Feeling faint, lightheaded, or very weak** along with stomach symptoms.

**Book a regular appointment with your doctor if:**

- You have heartburn two or more days a week, or you need antacids most weeks.
- Over-the-counter products aren't helping, or symptoms return as soon as you stop them.
- You have trouble or pain swallowing, food feels stuck, or you're losing weight without trying.
- Your stomach pain lingers for more than a few days after drinking.
- You notice that you're drinking more often or more heavily than you'd like. A doctor can help with that too, without judgment.

## Simple Habits That Mean You Need Antacids Less

The best antacid is the one you don't need. These habits help most people who get heartburn from drinking:

- **Eat a real meal before you drink**, but avoid very large, greasy, or spicy meals late at night.
- **Choose your drinks with your stomach in mind.** Many people find wine, beer, and fizzy mixed drinks worse than others. Notice what triggers you.
- **Pace yourself and alternate with water.** Less alcohol in a shorter window means less irritation.
- **Stop drinking and eating two to three hours before bed** if you can, so your stomach isn't full when you lie down.
- **Raise the head of your bed** or use an extra pillow if reflux keeps you up.
- **Don't smoke while drinking.** Smoking also relaxes the valve at the top of the stomach.

For the bigger picture on drinking in a way that leaves you feeling better the next day, see our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound that's sold as a hangover supplement. It is not an antacid and it won't stop heartburn. There's no good evidence that it protects your stomach lining or reduces acid reflux, so don't use it in place of the products above.

Where it's studied is alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of that research is in animals and cells, with limited human data, so it's promising rather than settled. Some people who drink socially like to take it alongside sensible habits. If you want to try it, two options we've reviewed are the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) and the more complete [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

If you take DHM and an antacid, the same pharmacist advice applies as for any supplement: ask whether to space them apart, especially if you also take prescription medicines.

## The Bottom Line

- **For quick relief of occasional heartburn after drinking:** Tums or a liquid antacid like Mylanta.
- **For acid coming up your throat at night:** Gaviscon, plus raising your head and not eating late.
- **To prevent predictable heartburn:** famotidine (Pepcid AC) taken beforehand, following the label.
- **For frequent heartburn:** a PPI like Prilosec OTC on its 14-day plan, and a conversation with your doctor.
- **Avoid after drinking:** original Alka-Seltzer (it contains aspirin), and be cautious with Pepto-Bismol and baking soda.
- **Never treat these with an antacid:** vomiting blood, black stools, severe pain into your back, or chest pain. Get care right away.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the best antacid after drinking alcohol?**

For occasional heartburn after a few drinks, a calcium carbonate antacid like Tums or a liquid aluminum/magnesium antacid like Mylanta gives the fastest relief. If acid is coming up into your throat, especially when you lie down, Gaviscon's alginate raft tends to work better. If you know drinking gives you heartburn, famotidine (Pepcid AC) taken beforehand, following the label, lasts longer. Ask a pharmacist first if you have kidney disease or take prescription medicines.

**Is it safe to take Tums after drinking?**

For most healthy adults, yes. There is no known dangerous interaction between calcium carbonate and alcohol. Stay within the daily maximum on the label, because it's easy to lose count after drinking, and very large amounts of calcium can cause problems. If you need Tums after most nights out, talk to your doctor.

**Which is better after drinking, Tums or Pepcid?**

They do different jobs. Tums neutralizes acid already in your stomach and works within minutes, but it wears off fairly quickly. Pepcid (famotidine) lowers acid production, takes up to an hour to start working, and lasts several hours. Tums is better for heartburn that's happening right now, and Pepcid is better taken ahead of time. Pepcid Complete combines both.

**Can I take Prilosec for heartburn after drinking?**

Prilosec OTC (omeprazole) isn't designed for fast relief. Its label describes a 14-day course for frequent heartburn, and it can take a few days to reach full effect. For a single rough night, a quick-acting antacid or Gaviscon is more useful. If you have heartburn two or more days a week, talk to a doctor about whether a PPI is right for you.

**Is Alka-Seltzer good for a hangover?**

Original Alka-Seltzer contains aspirin, which together with alcohol raises the risk of stomach irritation and bleeding. That makes it a poor choice when your stomach is already irritated from drinking. Some Alka-Seltzer products are aspirin-free, so read the Drug Facts box. For the stomach, a plain antacid is a gentler option.

**What helps alcohol gastritis fast?**

A plain antacid can ease the burning within minutes, and an H2 blocker like famotidine can reduce acid for several hours. The most important step is giving your stomach a few days without alcohol and avoiding aspirin and ibuprofen-type painkillers. If the pain lasts more than a few days or keeps coming back, see a doctor.

**When is stomach pain after drinking an emergency?**

Get emergency care if you vomit blood or coffee-ground material, pass black or tarry stools, have severe belly pain that spreads to your back, feel faint, or have chest pain with shortness of breath, sweating, or pain in your arm or jaw. These are not symptoms to treat with an antacid.

**Does DHM help with heartburn from drinking?**

There is no good evidence that DHM reduces heartburn or protects the stomach lining. It's studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver, mostly in animal research with limited human data. Use an appropriate antacid or acid reducer for heartburn, and follow the label.
